newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Romania's Greek Catholics still fight for churches.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Romania's Greek Catholics still fight for churches.

text.p: Every Sunday, winter or summer, hundreds of worshippers gather at a military monument in a park in the northern Romanian town of Baia Mare.
Dozens more congregate by a cross planted in a ditch in the village of Sisesti, a 15-minute drive down the highway.
All are members of the Greek Catholic faith, still without churches to pray in eight years after a communist-era ban on their three centuries-old faith was lifted.

"So far, we have won only the freedom to go public and hold our masses in the open air," said Ioan Sistean, one of Romania's six Greek Catholic bishops, after a religious service in which four priests were ordained.
"But even that after years of conspiracy and terror is a big step forward."

Romania's Greek Catholics, like their brethren in Ukraine and Poland, were forced underground in 1948 when pro-Moscow communists effectively liquidated their church after a year of relentless discrimination and oppression.
Seven of 12 bishops died after being thrown into prison and more than 2,000 church buildings were turned over to the majority Orthodox faith.
Some 2.5 million worshippers were told to join Orthodox parishes. Thousands who refused to recant were imprisoned.

A year after Nicolae Ceausescu's 1989 execution, the leftist government which took power formally lifted the ban. But no action was taken to secure the return of churches taken over by Orthodox parishes happy to hang on to the properties.
Official statistics show only 97 of the more than 2,000 churches and five cathedrals claimed by Greek Catholics have been returned and a total of 389 priests officiate at services.
DISPUTES LEAD TO VIOLENCE

As in Ukraine, disputes over churches claimed by Greek Catholics in the central Transylvania region have spilled over into periodic street battles. An attempt by the centrist government elected last year to calm passions has satisfied no one.
A bill before parliament proposes returning to Greek Catholics, who claim 1.7 million followers but officially number only 230,000, at least one church per village once under their control.

Orthodox clerics, who command the nominal allegiance of 86 percent of Romanians, said the bill amounted to interference in spiritual matters. Greek Catholics rejected it as inadequate, saying they wanted all their buildings back.

"It's not a law we need, but a presidential or governmental decree ordering the restitution of all our assets," said Sistean, ordained in a clandestine ceremony 25 years ago in the village house where he still lives.
"The communist state which took away our properties and handed them to the Orthodox must give them back to us."
Andrei Costinas, one of two priests serving in what is now Baia Mare's Orthodox cathedral, close to the Ukrainian border, says the legislation violates the church's autonomous status.
"The only thing we could agree to would be a referendum leaving the decision to be taken by parishioners," he said.
The Greek Catholic Church, also known as Uniate, came to Romania in 1700, more than a century after its foundation in 1596 in Brest by Orthodox seeking a return to papal control.
Its believers worship according to "eastern rites" virtually identical to Orthodox practices, but view the pope as their spiritual leader.
The church gained ground when much of modern-day Romania was under the control of the Austro-Hungarian empire as a bulwark against the advance of the Ottoman Turks.
PERSECUTION
Greek Catholics initially came under pressure when Romanian lands were reunited in 1918 and Orthodox clerics incited them to leave their faith.

Unlike Ukraine's five-million-strong Church, despised by Stalin because of its nationalist roots, Romania's Greek Catholics were persecuted by communist rulers because they were associated with "rotten Western imperialism".

In the aftermath of the war, nine out of 10 believers left the faith in a three-week campaign of intimidation. They were told that if they did not join Orthodox parishes they would lose their jobs, their children would be denied schooling and their grain would go unaccepted at village mills.
But hundreds defied the strict surveillance and harrassment of the Securitate secret police to attend clandestine services in private apartments or village houses.
Greek Catholics have begun building new churches to give believers a proper place to gather, but carry on their fight to recover what they say was built by their forebears decades or centuries ago.

"We're legal now, but we cannot function because we have no place to go," said Cristina Ciociltisan, one of 500 Greek Catholics in Sisesti -- nearly half the village's population -- reduced to praying each week in the ditch.
"We stand here by the road while the Greek Catholic priest who built the village church is buried inside where Orthodox are praying. Surely, he cannot be at rest after all this time."
But attitudes remain entrenched. Many Orthodox say they have no intention of returning property they looked after for 50 years during the darkest repressions of communism.
"They abandoned the church and we took care of it for years," said one woman in her seventies. "Now they're asking for it back? No way."
